s: Which High Courts exercised writ jurisdiction before 1950?
x: Before 1950 only the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction; Article 226 now empowers all High Courts.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the writs named in Article 32(2)?
x: Article 32(2) names five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto; injunction is not one of them.

s: Under which system did the writ remedies of the Supreme Court and High Courts originate as prerogative remedies?
x: The writs come from the prerogative remedies of English common law and are exercised under Articles 32 and 226.

s: Against whom may the writ of Habeas Corpus be issued?
o: Both public authorities and private individuals
x: Habeas Corpus lies against public authorities and private individuals for unlawful detention; it does not require release where detention is lawful.

s: Against the holder of which office does the writ of Quo Warranto lie?
o: A substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution
Any office in a private trust
x: Quo Warranto tests a claim to a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution and may be sought by any interested person.

s: Which writ quashes an order already passed by an inferior court?
x: Certiorari quashes an order already passed; prohibition prevents an order from being made.

s: Which of the following writs is included in the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32?
x: Under Article 32, the Court can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. Review, advisory opinions and special leave are other kinds of jurisdiction.

s: Which writ is directed against judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies to quash an illegal order suffering from lack or excess of jurisdiction or an error of law apparent on the face of the record?
x: Certiorari quashes an order already passed by a judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative body for lack or excess of jurisdiction or error of law on the record. Prohibition acts earlier, while proceedings are pending.

s: Which of the following writs is correctly matched with its meaning?
o: Habeas Corpus – To forbid or restrain
Mandamus – To be certified or informed
Certiorari – To be certified or informed
x: Certiorari means 'to be certified or informed'; Habeas Corpus means 'to have the body', Mandamus 'we command' and Prohibition 'to forbid'.

s: On which ground may a writ of certiorari be issued?
o: Illegal usurpation of a public office
Error of law on the face of the record
Refusal to perform a public duty
x: Certiorari lies for lack or excess of jurisdiction or error of law on the face of the record.

s: Which writ directs a lower judicial body to stop continuing proceedings in excess of its jurisdiction?
x: Prohibition prevents continuation of proceedings, while certiorari quashes an order; both check jurisdictional excess by judicial or quasi-judicial bodies.

s: Which writ is called the 'bulwark of individual liberty'?
x: Habeas Corpus is the bulwark of individual liberty: it frees a person from unlawful detention quickly.

s: Which of the following is correct about Article 32?
o: It is a statutory remedy that Parliament may withdraw
It can be repealed by amendment as it is merely procedural
It is part of the basic structure and cannot be abridged by amendment
It applies only to rights created by ordinary law
x: Article 32 is part of the basic structure, so its essential guarantee cannot be abridged even by a constitutional amendment.

s: The saying 'A right without a remedy is a worthless declaration' explains the importance of which Article?
x: Article 32 gives a direct constitutional remedy for enforcing Fundamental Rights, making Part III effective rather than merely declaratory.

s: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar describe Article 32 as the “heart and soul of the Constitution”?
o: It empowers the President to issue constitutional writs
It guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies
It gives Parliament power to amend Fundamental Rights
It establishes the jurisdiction of High Courts over statutory rights
x: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it makes the right to a remedy itself a Fundamental Right, giving direct access to the Supreme Court.

s: How many judges decided Kesavananda Bharati, which made judicial review under Articles 32, 226 and 227 basic structure?
x: Kesavananda Bharati was a 13-judge Bench.

s: Who described Article 32 as 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'?
x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the very soul and heart of the Constitution.

s: Which Article of the Constitution gives the power of judicial review to the Supreme Court and the High Courts?
x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void, giving the Supreme Court and High Courts the power of judicial review.

s: In which case was the writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 held to be part of the basic structure?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997
x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.

s: What is the nature of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32?
x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.

s: The Supreme Court is described as the 'protector and guarantor' of which of the following?
x: The Supreme Court is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights; the Judiciary is their guardian.

s: High Courts have wider writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court because, under Article 226, they can issue writs for what?
o: Legal rights only, not Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights only, but against private bodies
x: Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose', while the Supreme Court under Article 32 acts only for Fundamental Rights.

s: When may a High Court issue a writ beyond its territorial limits under Article 226?
o: the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises within its territory
the Union Government transfers the proceeding to it
the Supreme Court authorises it in every individual case
the respondent is located anywhere in India, irrespective of cause of action
x: A High Court ordinarily exercises Article 226 jurisdiction within its territory, but may do so beyond that territory where the cause of action wholly or partly arises within its territorial jurisdiction. This position followed the Fifteenth Amendment of 1963.

s: How many writs can a High Court issue under Article 226?
x: Both the Supreme Court and the High Courts can issue all five writs.

s: In which matters has the Supreme Court examined an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Articles 32 and 226?
x: The proposed SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings concerns threats to life and liberty, strengthening access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.

s: If a High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits, what is the position of an Article 32 petition on the same plea?
o: Maintainable, as Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right
Automatically converted into an Article 226 petition
Barred by res judicata; the remedy lies in appeal
Maintainable, as res judicata applies only to civil suits
x: After a dismissal on merits, the same plea ordinarily cannot be raised under Article 32; the remedy is an appeal. If the dismissal was not on merits, Article 32 may be invoked.

s: Which Amendment inserted Article 32A, which barred challenges to State laws under Article 32?
x: The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 32A; the 43rd Amendment omitted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A.

s: In January 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to examine which question in appeals by Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling?
o: Whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction
Whether High Courts can issue writs of quo warranto against Ministers
Whether Article 32 can be suspended during a financial emergency
Whether Parliament can empower district courts to issue writs under Article 32(3)
x: On 20 January 2026, a Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction. The appeals came from Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling. The other three options are not what was referred.

s: Which Amendment omitted Article 32A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment?
x: The 43rd Amendment (1977) omitted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A.

s: Since which Amendment may High Courts issue writs beyond their territory where the cause of action arises within it?
x: The 15th Amendment (1963) let High Courts issue writs beyond their territory if the cause of action arises within it.

s: In what respect is the writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32?
x: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose', so their subject-matter scope is wider, while the Supreme Court's is wider territorially.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The remedy under Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
2. The remedy under Article 226 is a discretionary remedy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right that the Supreme Court cannot refuse, while Article 226 is a discretionary constitutional remedy.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Quo Warranto?
o: It literally means 'by what authority or warrant'
Only a person personally aggrieved can seek it
Any member of the public can move a petition for it
It is one of the writs named in Article 32(2)
x: Any public-spirited person, not only an aggrieved one, may seek Quo Warranto.

s: Which of the following pairs (writ – primary target) is wrongly matched?
o: Habeas Corpus – Public authorities and private individuals
Mandamus – Private individuals as a general rule
Prohibition – Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only
Quo Warranto – Person holding or claiming a substantive public office
x: Mandamus lies against public officials, statutory bodies, inferior courts and tribunals, not ordinarily against private individuals.

s: In respect of which office does Quo Warranto NOT lie?
x: Quo Warranto tests claims to substantive public offices created by statute or the Constitution, not ministerial or private offices.

s: In which of the following cases is the writ of habeas corpus NOT issued?
o: Illegal confinement by a private person
x: Habeas corpus does not lie for lawful detention, contempt of court or legislature, or detention outside the court's jurisdiction.

s: Since 1991, against which of the following may the writ of Certiorari also lie?
o: Certain administrative bodies when their actions affect rights
The President and Governor for their official acts
x: The scope of Certiorari has been extended to certain administrative bodies whose decisions affect rights. It does not ordinarily lie against private persons or legislative bodies.

s: What can a court do through the writ of mandamus?
o: Compel the Government to formulate a policy
Direct the Government to enact a law
Issue directions only against private individuals
Enforce the terms of a policy once laid down
x: Mandamus cannot compel the Government to make a law or policy, but can enforce a policy once laid down.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mandamus?
o: It compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty
It lies against the President and Governors
It may lie against a government company performing a public function
x: Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors (or private bodies without public duties), though it can lie against government companies performing public functions.

s: Mandamus can lie against which of the following when it is performing a public function?
o: A purely private body discharging no public duty
A Governor acting in the discharge of office
A government company or statutory corporation
x: Mandamus lies against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function. It does not lie against the President, Governors or purely private bodies.

s: Because of which Article can mandamus not be issued against the President or Governors?
x: Article 361 says the President and Governors are not answerable to any court for official acts.

s: Against which of the following does the writ of prohibition NOT lie?
x: Prohibition lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, not administrative authorities.

s: As a general rule, against whom does the writ of mandamus NOT lie?
o: A public official refusing a public duty
x: Mandamus is not ordinarily issued against private bodies; it lies against public officials, inferior courts and tribunals.

s: The writ of mandamus cannot be issued to enforce which of the following?
o: A public legal duty refused by an official
A statutory duty of a public corporation
A duty neglected by a tribunal
x: Mandamus does not lie to enforce a contractual obligation, a discretionary duty or non-statutory instructions.

s: Against which of the following does the writ of certiorari NOT lie?
x: Certiorari does not lie against legislative bodies or private persons.

s: Besides quashing an order already passed, for what else may the writ of certiorari be used?
o: Compel performance of a public duty
Remove a usurper of public office
x: Certiorari is generally post-decision but may also be used to transfer a pending case.

s: What kind of writ is Prohibition, as it operates while the lower proceeding is still pending?
x: Prohibition is preventive as it acts while the case is pending, while certiorari is curative as it acts after an order is made.

s:
Consider the following statements about prohibition and certiorari:
1. Prohibition is preventive only.
2. Certiorari is both preventive and curative.
3. Certiorari is nicknamed 'postmortem'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: prohibition only prevents, while certiorari also cures by quashing an order and is called 'postmortem'.

s: Which of the following is common to the writs of prohibition and certiorari?
o: Both are issued only after the final order
Both check a lower body's excess of jurisdiction
Both compel performance of a public duty
x: Prohibition and certiorari both check excess of jurisdiction by judicial and quasi-judicial bodies; prohibition acts while proceedings are pending, certiorari after the order.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 32?
o: Clause (1) makes the right to move the Supreme Court for Part III rights itself a Fundamental Right
Under clause (2), the Supreme Court may issue directions, orders or writs
Under clause (4), the right may be suspended by an ordinary law of Parliament
Clause (4) says the right shall not be suspended except as the Constitution provides
x: Article 32(4) says the right cannot be suspended except as the Constitution provides, not by an ordinary law.

s: Which provision lets Parliament empower any other court to exercise the Supreme Court's powers under Article 32?
x: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower other courts, though no such law has been made; High Courts issue writs under Article 226.

s: Has Parliament made a law under Article 32(3) empowering other courts to exercise writ powers?
o: No, no such law has been made
x: Article 32(3) allows Parliament to empower other courts, but no such law has been made yet.

s: Why can a violation of the right to property not be challenged by a writ under Article 32?
o: Property is now a legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right
Only Parliament can decide property disputes
Property disputes go only to Lok Adalats
x: Article 32 enforces only Fundamental Rights; property is now a legal right under Article 300A, enforced through Article 226 or a suit.

s: Under Article 359, the President cannot suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of which Articles?
x: During a National Emergency, enforcement of named FRs may be suspended, except Articles 20 and 21.

s: Which Amendment protected Articles 20 and 21 from suspension during an emergency?
x: The 44th Amendment barred suspension of Articles 20 and 21 under Article 359.

s: Who may restrict or modify the Fundamental Rights of armed forces personnel under Article 33?
x: Under Article 33 only Parliament, not State legislatures, may restrict FRs of armed forces, police and intelligence personnel.

s: Which Article provides for restrictions on Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force?
x: Article 34 deals with martial law; Parliament may indemnify acts done under it.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Articles 33-35?
o: Under Article 35, Parliament alone legislates on specified FR matters
State legislatures may modify the Fundamental Rights of police under Article 33
Article 33 covers armed forces, police and intelligence personnel
Parliament may indemnify acts done under martial law under Article 34
x: Article 33 power belongs to Parliament, not State legislatures.

s: Public Interest Litigation primarily relaxes which traditional rule?
o: The rule that courts cannot issue writs against public authorities
The rule that Fundamental Rights are enforceable only by Parliament
The rule that judicial review is unavailable against administrative action
The rule that only the directly aggrieved person may approach the court
x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi by permitting a public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so themselves or for a larger public interest.

s: Which 1981 case is associated with the development of Public Interest Litigation?
x: S.P. Gupta (1981) is a key PIL case; Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer are associated with PIL.

s: Under epistolary jurisdiction, in which case was a prisoner's letter treated as a writ petition?
x: Epistolary jurisdiction treats letters or postcards as writ petitions; Sunil Batra, where a prisoner's letter was acted upon, is the example.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Public Interest Litigation?
o: Any public-spirited person may move the court
S.P. Gupta (1981) is a key PIL case
It is itself a Fundamental Right
It relaxes the rule of locus standi
x: PIL loosens locus standi but is not itself a Fundamental Right.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to secure a living wage and promote cottage industries?
x: Article 43 covers living wage and cottage industries; 39A is free legal aid, 41 right to work and 42 humane work conditions.

s: Separation of the judiciary from the executive is directed by which Article?
x: Article 50 directs separation of the judiciary from the executive; international peace and security is Article 51.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to organise village panchayats?
x: Article 40 covers village panchayats; 39A is free legal aid, 43 living wage and cottage industries, and 44 the Uniform Civil Code.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Equal justice and free legal aid – Article 39A
x: Article 39A provides for equal justice and free legal aid. Humane conditions of work are Article 42, the Uniform Civil Code is Article 44 and environment protection is Article 48A.

s: Which of the following statements regarding the Directive Principles is incorrect?
o: Article 48A provides for the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive.
Article 50 deals with the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive.
Article 44 deals with the Uniform Civil Code.
Article 39A provides for equal justice and free legal aid.
x: A is incorrect: Article 48A is about protecting and improving the environment, forests and wildlife; separation of the judiciary from the executive is Article 50. Articles 44 (UCC) and 39A (free legal aid) are stated correctly.

s: Which Article of the Directive Principles provides for the prohibition of slaughter of cows and calves?
x: The cow-slaughter ban is in Article 48; Article 46 promotes the interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections.

s: Which of the following pairs (Article – Directive) is wrongly matched?
o: Article 45 – Originally, free and compulsory education up to 14 years
Article 48 – Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
Article 48A – Safeguarding of forests and wildlife
x: Article 49 concerns protection of monuments and places of national importance; the Uniform Civil Code is Article 44.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections — Article 46
x: C is correct: Article 46 protects the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections. The others are mismatched: village panchayats are Art. 40 (not 43), cottage industries are Art. 43 (not 40), and prohibition of intoxicating drinks is Art. 47 (not 48).

s: Which Article of the Constitution deals with a social order based on social, economic and political justice and the minimisation of inequalities?
x: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order informed by justice and to minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities.

s: Which one of the following correctly states the subject matter of Articles 39(b) and 39(c)?
o: 39(b): distribution of community resources for the common good; 39(c): prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production
39(b): protection of monuments; 39(c): promotion of international peace
39(b): right to work; 39(c): free legal aid
x: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community to subserve the common good, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.

s: Which one of the following correctly matches the constitutional provision with its nature?
o: Article 24 — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 39(f) — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 21A — Directive Principle of State Policy
x: Article 39(f) is a Directive Principle of State Policy. Articles 24 and 21A are Fundamental Rights, while Article 39(e) is also a Directive Principle.

s: After the constitutional changes relating to education, what does Article 45 direct the State to provide?
o: Free legal aid to all citizens
Early childhood care and education until six years of age
Free and compulsory education from six to fourteen years
x: Article 45 now covers early childhood care and education until six; education from six to fourteen is the Fundamental Right under Article 21A.

s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief?
x: Article 42 covers humane conditions of work and maternity relief; 38 is welfare of the people, 39 livelihood and equal pay, 41 right to work.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Article 43 provides for a living wage and a decent standard of life.
Article 47 directs the State to raise the level of nutrition, raise the standard of living and improve public health.
Article 43A directs the State to provide for the participation of workers in the management of agriculture.
Article 43A provides for the participation of workers in the management of industries.
x: C is incorrect: Article 43A provides for workers' participation in the management of industries, not agriculture. Articles 43 (living wage) and 47 (nutrition, public health) are stated correctly.

s: Article 43A provides for participation of workers in the management of which of the following?
x: Article 43A, added by the 42nd Amendment, concerns workers' participation in the management of industries, not agriculture.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to secure the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement?
x: Article 41 deals with the right to work, to education and to public assistance.

s: Which Article of the Directive Principles directs the State to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health?
x: Article 47 covers nutrition, public health and prohibition of intoxicating drinks and injurious drugs.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to protect monuments and places of national importance?
x: Article 49, a Directive Principle, provides for the protection of monuments and places of national importance.

s: Which is the last Article of Part IV of the Constitution, dealing with the promotion of international peace and security?
x: Article 51, the last Article of Part IV, deals with international peace and security and respect for international law.

s: What does Article 39(a) of the Constitution direct the State to secure?
o: The right to work in every circumstance
Free legal aid to economically weaker citizens
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
Adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally
x: Article 39(a) directs the State to secure adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally. Equal pay for equal work is contained in Article 39(d).

s: Which clause of Article 39 protects children against exploitation and abandonment and provides for their development in freedom and dignity?
x: Article 39(f) directs that children should develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and be protected against exploitation and abandonment. The present wording was introduced through the 42nd Amendment.

s: Which clause of Article 39 provides for equal pay for equal work for both men and women?
x: Article 39(d) deals with equal pay; 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers and children from unsuited work.

s: Which clause of Article 39 directs that the tender age of children and the health of workers are not abused?
x: Article 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers and the tender age of children; 39(d) is equal pay for equal work.

s: Which of the following is NOT a Directive Principle of State Policy?
x: The Right to Information is a legal right under the RTI Act, 2005; right to work (41), UCC (44) and maternity relief (42) are DPSPs.

s: Which of the following is a Directive Principle and NOT a Fundamental Right under the Constitution?
o: Right to education for children aged 6-14
x: The right to work is a Directive Principle under Article 41, not a Fundamental Right. Education for 6-14 (Art. 21A), forced labour ban (Art. 23) and equality (Art. 14) are Fundamental Rights.

s: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
x: The DPSPs are in Part IV (Articles 36–51); they are fundamental in governance but not enforceable by courts.

s: Article 36 of the Constitution deals with which of the following?
o: Application of the Directive Principles of State Policy
Social order and minimisation of inequalities
x: Article 36 defines 'State' for Part IV (as Article 12 does for Part III). Article 37 makes DPSP non-justiciable; 38 and 39 set the welfare and policy goals.

s: How many Articles does Part IV (Articles 36-51) contain?
x: Part IV runs from Article 36 to Article 51, i.e. 16 articles.

s: What do the Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish?
o: Social and economic democracy and a welfare state
x: The DPSPs aim at social democracy, economic democracy and a welfare state; the idea was borrowed from Ireland.

s: What is the sanction behind the Directive Principles of State Policy?
x: FRs carry a legal sanction enforced by courts, while DPSPs carry a moral and political sanction.

s: Courts have generally used the Directive Principles of State Policy in which of the following ways?
o: As independently enforceable rights replacing Fundamental Rights
As provisions applicable exclusively to local governments
As limitations that prevent all legislative action under Part III
As interpretive aids, including in reading certain principles into Article 21
x: Although DPSPs are not independently enforceable, courts use them as interpretive aids and have read several welfare-oriented principles into the scope of Article 21.

s: Directive Principles generally impose which kind of obligation on the State?
o: Positive obligations requiring the State to act
x: Directive Principles generally require the State to undertake welfare measures, while Fundamental Rights mostly restrain the State.

s:
Assertion (A): The Directive Principles cannot be enforced by any court.
Reason (R): Article 37 makes the Directive Principles non-justiciable.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: courts cannot enforce the Directive Principles because Article 37 declares them non-justiciable, though fundamental in governance.

s: According to the Minerva Mills case (1980), what is the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: Part IV is absolutely superior to Part III
A balance between Part III and Part IV is part of the Basic Structure
Part III is absolutely superior to Part IV
Both Part III and Part IV are outside judicial review
x: The balance and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the Basic Structure; neither Part has unlimited supremacy.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Fundamental Rights – Moral and political sanction
x: Fundamental Rights aim at political democracy and carry legal sanction; DPSPs are non-justiciable with moral and political sanction.

s: From which of the following does the non-enforceability of the Directive Principles in courts arise?
o: The ideal of international peace in Article 51
The aim of a welfare state in Article 38
x: Non-enforceability arises from the express bar in Article 37, not merely from their role as a guide to law-making.

s: Which of the following was NOT added to the Directive Principles by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
o: Article 39A – Equal justice and free legal aid
x: Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978; the 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A, 48A and 39(f).

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Article 40 deals with the organisation of Village Panchayats.
Article 50 deals with the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive.
Article 43B was added by the 42nd Amendment.
Article 46 promotes the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections.
x: C is incorrect: Article 43B (co-operative societies) was added by the 97th Amendment (2011), not the 42nd. The others are right: Article 40 panchayats, 50 separation of judiciary, 46 weaker sections.

s: By which Amendment was the Ninth Schedule added to the Constitution?
x: The First Amendment, 1951 introduced the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B; the 73rd Amendment dealt with Panchayati Raj.

s:
Arrange the following changes to the Directive Principles in chronological order:
A. Insertion of Article 43B (co-operative societies)
B. Substitution of Article 45 (early childhood care and education)
C. Insertion of Articles 39A, 43A and 48A
D. Insertion of Article 38(2) (minimising inequalities)
x: 42nd Amendment (1976) added 39A, 43A, 48A; 44th (1978) added 38(2); 86th (2002) substituted Article 45; 97th (2011) added Article 43B.

s: By which Amendment was Article 38(2) added to the Directive Principles?
x: Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978; Article 43B came by the 97th (2011) and the present Article 45 by the 86th (2002).

s: Article 43B on co-operative societies was added by which Amendment?
x: The 97th Amendment, 2011 added Article 43B, the last DPSP added.

s:
Consider the following statements about amendments to the Directive Principles:
1. The 44th Amendment added Article 38(2).
2. The 86th Amendment substituted Article 45.
3. The 42nd Amendment added Article 44.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 44th added 38(2) and the 86th substituted Article 45; the UCC (Article 44) was not added by the 42nd Amendment.

s: On which date did Article 39A on free legal aid come into force?
x: Article 39A was added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment and came into force on 3 January 1977; 9 November 1995 is when the Legal Services Authorities Act came into force.

s: Article 48 directs the State to ban the slaughter of cows and calves. Under which entry does the power to legislate on this subject lie?
x: Article 48 is only a directive; the power to legislate on cow slaughter lies with the States under State List Entry 15 (livestock).

s: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 support which Directive Principle?
x: Article 48A is supported by wildlife and environmental legislation; Article 47 is reflected in public health measures such as the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about recent developments on Article 44?
o: In Pavini Shukla v. Union of India (2026), the Supreme Court suggested a UCC to end gender discrimination
Article 44 is enforceable in court like a Fundamental Right
In March 2026 a three-judge Bench considered deferring to Parliament on Article 44
Article 44 is a Directive Principle with no legal force
x: Article 44 is a DPSP with no legal force and is not enforceable like a Fundamental Right.

s: MGNREGA, 2005, linked to Article 41, has been replaced by which Act?
x: MGNREGA was replaced by the VB-GRAM G Act; a sharp fall in employment under it has revived the right-to-work debate.

s: Which group is exempted from the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2026?
x: Scheduled Tribes are exempted. Gujarat is the second State after Uttarakhand to move a UCC, providing for monogamy and equal inheritance.

s: The Legal Services Authorities Act, which implements Article 39A, came into force on 9 November of which year?
x: The Act of 1987 came into force on 9 November 1995, observed as National Legal Services Day; it sets up NALSA, SLSAs and DLSAs.

s: Through which of the following was Article 40 (organisation of village panchayats) implemented?
x: Article 40 was given effect by the 73rd Amendment, 1992; the RTE Act implements Articles 45/21A.

s: Goa’s civil-law system is based on which of the following?
o: The Uniform Civil Code enacted by Parliament
x: Goa follows the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867, making it a distinctive example in discussions concerning a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44.

s: Which State was the first to adopt a State Uniform Civil Code?
x: Uttarakhand was the first State with a UCC and Gujarat the second; Goa follows the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867.

s: When was the National Social Assistance Programme, which meets the directive of Article 41, launched?
x: The NSAP was launched on 15 August 1995 and serves the directives on right to work, education and public assistance (Article 41).

s: Which of the following days is observed on 9 November, the day the Legal Services Authorities Act came into force in 1995?
x: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 came into force on 9 November 1995, so 9 November is National Legal Services Day.

s: Which Directive Principle is given effect by the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), which organises Lok Adalats?
x: NALSA was formed under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which implements Article 39A on equal justice and free legal aid.

s: Which State became the second State, after Uttarakhand, to move a State Uniform Civil Code?
x: Uttarakhand was the first State with a UCC and Gujarat the second; Goa follows the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867.

s: Which Law Commission, headed by Justice B.S. Chauhan, said in 2018 that a Uniform Civil Code was 'neither necessary nor desirable'?
x: The 21st Law Commission under Justice B.S. Chauhan said in 2018 that a UCC was neither necessary nor desirable.

s: Which Act gives effect to Article 45 and Article 21A by providing free education to children aged 6-14 in a neighbourhood school?
o: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
x: The RTE Act, 2009 (Section 3) provides free education to children aged 6-14 in a neighbourhood school.

s: Land reforms such as zamindari abolition and ceiling laws were enacted mainly to implement which Directive Principles?
x: Land reforms give effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) on distribution of material resources and preventing concentration of wealth.

s: The Directive Principles are referred to by which of the following expressions?
o: Instrument of Governance and Charter of the Constitution
Instrument of Instructions and Conscience of the Constitution
Instrument of Rights and Conscience of the Judiciary
Conscience of Parliament and Legal Instructions
x: DPSP are called the 'Instrument of Instructions' (like those under the 1935 Act) and the 'conscience of the Constitution' (Granville Austin).

s: The Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution were modelled directly on the Constitution of which country?
x: India took the idea from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had itself copied it from the Spanish Constitution.

s: Under which Act was the Instrument of Instructions, an antecedent of the Directive Principles, found?
x: The Instrument of Instructions under the 1935 Act and the Karachi Resolution (1931) are antecedents of the DPSPs.

s: From the Constitution of which country did Ireland borrow the idea of Directive Principles?
x: India borrowed the DPSPs from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had copied the idea from Spain.

s: Which body split rights into justiciable and non-justiciable categories?
x: The Sapru Committee (1945) divided rights into justiciable and non-justiciable ones, an antecedent of Part IV.

s: Which of the following antecedents of the Directive Principles gave the socialist-nationalist economic programme of the freedom struggle?
x: The Karachi Resolution of 1931 set out the socialist-nationalist economic programme of the freedom struggle, an Indian precursor of the DPSPs.

s: In which year was the Karachi Resolution, an Indian precursor of the Directive Principles, adopted?
x: The Karachi Resolution was adopted in 1931; the Nehru Report was 1928 and the Sapru Committee 1945.

s: What were the Directive Principles called in the Irish Constitution of 1937, from which India borrowed them?
x: The Irish Constitution of 1937 called them 'Directive Principles of Social Policy'.

s: Before August 2019, which of the following Parts of the Constitution of India did not apply to the State of Jammu and Kashmir?
o: Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy
Part XI - Relations between the Union and the States
x: Under the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954, Part IV (DPSP) was not applicable to J&K, while Part III applied with modifications.

s: By which Presidential order of 5 August 2019 were all the provisions of the Constitution, including the Directive Principles, applied to Jammu and Kashmir?
o: Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954
Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019 (C.O. 272)
Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019
x: C.O. 272 of 5 August 2019 superseded the 1954 Order and applied all provisions of the Constitution to J&K.

s: Which of the following descriptions of the Directive Principles is an approving one, not a criticism?
o: No better than New Year's resolutions
A novel feature of the Indian Constitution
x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution; the other remarks criticise their non-justiciable character.

s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'a manifesto of aims and aspirations'?
x: K.C. Wheare called them a manifesto of aims and aspirations; Ivor Jennings called them 'pious aspirations' and T.T. Krishnamachari 'a veritable dustbin of sentiments'.

s: The debate over the right to work as a Fundamental Right versus a Directive Principle was associated in the Constituent Assembly with which pair?
o: K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar
Rajendra Prasad and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
N. Rau and K. M. Munshi
x: The Constituent Assembly debate on whether the right to work should be a Fundamental Right or remain a Directive Principle involved K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar.

s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'a veritable dustbin of sentiments'?
x: 'Dustbin of sentiments' was T.T. Krishnamachari's phrase; Granville Austin called FRs and DPSPs the conscience of the Constitution.

s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'pious aspirations'?
x: Ivor Jennings called them pious aspirations; K.T. Shah compared them to a cheque payable at the bank's convenience.

s: Who called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution?
x: Ambedkar's 'novel feature' is the only approving remark; K.C. Wheare called them a manifesto of aims and aspirations.

s: Who said that the Directive Principles were 'no better than New Year's resolutions' which are broken on the second of January?
x: Nasiruddin compared the DPSPs to New Year's resolutions broken on the second of January.

s: Who described the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles together as the 'conscience of the Constitution'?
x: Granville Austin called the FRs and DPSPs together the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

s: Which of the following Directive Principles is a liberal-intellectual principle rather than a Gandhian one?
x: Article 50 (separation of judiciary) is liberal-intellectual; Articles 40, 43B, 46 and 48 are Gandhian.

s: How many Articles make up the Liberal-intellectual group of Directive Principles?
x: The Liberal-intellectual group has seven Articles, including 44 (UCC), 45, 48 and 48A.

s: Which of the following Directive Principles is grouped under the Gandhian, not the Socialist, principles?
x: Article 43B (co-operative societies) is Gandhian; Articles 38, 39A and 47 are generally grouped under Socialist principles.

s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of Articles generally classified as Gandhian principles?
x: Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46 are generally included among Gandhian principles. The other sets contain Socialist or Liberal-intellectual principles.

s: Which of the following is true of the classification of Directive Principles into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual groups?
o: An academic arrangement used for study
Made by the Supreme Court in Part IV
x: The Constitution does not itself classify the Directive Principles; the three-fold grouping is an academic arrangement.

s: How many Articles are counted in the Gandhian group of Directive Principles?
x: The Gandhian group has six Articles: 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47 and 48.

s: Article 43B (co-operative societies) falls under which group of Directive Principles?
x: Article 43B is a Gandhian principle; Articles 38, 39A and 47 are in the Socialistic group.

s: Environmental protection is provided under which provision as a Fundamental Duty?
x: Protecting the environment is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g). Article 48A makes it a Directive Principle, not a duty.

s: Which Article provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities?
x: The Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities is under Article 350B; Article 350A concerns mother-tongue education.

s: Heritage and monuments are covered by Article 49. Which Fundamental Duty also covers them?
x: Article 49 and Article 51A(f) relate to heritage; Article 45 pairs with 51A(k) on education, and Article 39 with 51A(e) on women's dignity.

s: Which Article, a directive outside Part IV, deals with the development of Hindi?
x: Article 351 covers development of Hindi and Article 335 SC/ST claims to services; both are non-justiciable directives outside Part IV.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage?
x: Article 350A, outside Part IV, directs mother-tongue instruction; 350B provides a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

s: Article 335, a directive outside Part IV, is related to which of the following?
o: Mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage
Claims of SCs and STs to services
x: Article 335 deals with claims of SCs and STs to services, consistent with efficiency of administration; Hindi is Article 351.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Protection of the environment, forests and wildlife appears both as a Directive Principle and as a Fundamental Duty.
2. Free legal aid is a Fundamental Duty of every citizen under Article 51A.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Environment is in DPSP Article 48A (duty of the State) and FD Article 51A(g) (duty of citizens). Free legal aid is DPSP Article 39A, not a Fundamental Duty.

s: Which of the following is found in the Directive Principles but has no matching Fundamental Duty in Article 51A?
o: Preserving the heritage of composite culture
Equal justice and free legal aid
x: Free legal aid is only a Directive Principle (Article 39A). Environment (51A(g)), heritage (51A(f)) and education (51A(k)) also appear as Fundamental Duties.

s: Which was the first case of conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
x: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) was the first conflict case; I.R. Coelho (2007) was the last word on the Ninth Schedule.

s: Which case adopted the doctrine of harmonious construction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
x: Harmonious construction came in In re Kerala Education Bill (1958); Champakam (1951) held that Fundamental Rights prevail.

s: Which case denied Parliament the power to amend Fundamental Rights and applied the doctrine of prospective overruling?
x: Golaknath (1967) gave FRs a 'transcendental' position and applied prospective overruling; 'amendable but not the Basic Structure' is Kesavananda Bharati.

s: In which year was Minerva Mills decided?
x: Minerva Mills (1980) came after Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and before Sanjeev Coke (1983).

s: Which 1950 case gave a narrow interpretation of Article 21?
o: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
x: A.K. Gopalan (1950) read Article 21 narrowly; Golaknath (1967) barred amendment of FRs and Kesavananda (1973) protected the basic structure.

s: Which landmark case expanded the scope of Article 21 through due process?
x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 by requiring the procedure to be fair, just and reasonable (due process). A.K. Gopalan (1950) read it narrowly; Golaknath and Minerva Mills dealt with amending power.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Minerva Mills (1980) – Fundamental Rights are superior to DPSP
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) – Balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP
Golaknath (1967) – Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
x: Golaknath held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. Champakam: FRs above DPSP; Kesavananda: Basic Structure; Minerva Mills: balance between FRs and DPSP.

s: How many judges heard the Kesavananda Bharati case?
x: Kesavananda had a 13-judge bench, the largest; Golaknath had 11.

s: Which of the following cases was decided after Minerva Mills (1980)?
x: Sanjeev Coke came in 1983, after Minerva Mills; the others are earlier (1951, 1967, 1973).

s: In re Kerala Education Bill, 1958 is associated with which of the following approaches?
o: Harmonious construction, giving effect to both Fundamental Rights and DPSPs as far as possible
Parliament's inability to amend any Fundamental Right
Complete supremacy of DPSPs over Fundamental Rights
x: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, requiring both Parts III and IV to be given effect as far as possible, while Fundamental Rights continued to prevail in case of direct conflict.

s: Which of the following famous cases is related to personal liberty under Article 21 and not to the Right to Property or the amending power?
x: Maneka Gandhi widened Article 21 by requiring a fair, just and reasonable procedure. Golaknath and Kesavananda dealt with property and amending power; Sanjeev Coke with Article 39(b).

s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Minerva Mills
B. In re Kerala Education Bill
C. Sanjeev Coke
D. Golaknath
x: Kerala Education Bill (1958), Golaknath (1967), Minerva Mills (1980), Sanjeev Coke (1983).

s: Article 15(4), inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951, was a response to which judgment?
x: Article 15(4) answered Champakam Dorairajan; Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule answered the land-reform judgments.

s: Article 15(4) was the response to the Champakam Dorairajan case. The bar under which Article did it overcome?
x: Champakam struck down a communal order under Article 29(2); the 1st Amendment inserted Article 15(4) in response.

s: For whom does Article 15(4) enable special provisions?
o: Socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs
x: Article 15(4), inserted by the 1st Amendment, 1951, provides for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.

s: Fundamental Rights are mostly ____, while Directive Principles are positive directions to the State.
x: FRs are mostly negative and aim at political democracy; DPSPs are positive and aim at social and economic democracy.

s: A law violating a Fundamental Right and a law violating a Directive Principle have which respective legal consequences?
o: The former may be void under Article 13, while the latter cannot be struck down merely for violating a Directive Principle
The former cannot be examined by courts, while the latter is void under Article 37
Both laws are automatically void under Article 13
Both laws are immune from judicial review
x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency. Courts cannot strike down a law solely because it violates a Directive Principle.

s: What does Article 37 declare the Directive Principles to be?
o: Enforceable only during a national emergency
Fundamental in the governance of the country
x: Article 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in the governance of the country, and the State must apply them in making laws.

s: If Fundamental Rights are the means, what are the Directive Principles described as?
x: Fundamental Rights provide the means through which the social and economic goals (ends) of the Directive Principles are pursued.

s: Which of the following may be invoked to determine the ambit of both Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
x: The Preamble states the aims of the Constitution, so it may be used to decide the ambit of both Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

s: In which year was the First Constitutional Amendment Act, which added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule, enacted?
x: The 1st Amendment (1951) added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to protect land-reform and welfare laws from early court rulings.

s: By which Amendment were Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule inserted?
x: The First Amendment, 1951 created Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield land-reform laws; the Schedule later grew to over 280 entries.

s: In Waman Rao (1981), laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after which date were held open to challenge?
x: Waman Rao used 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda judgment, as the cut-off; I.R. Coelho (2007) rejected blanket immunity.

s: In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), which Articles make up the 'golden triangle' test for Ninth Schedule laws?
x: I.R. Coelho held there is no blanket immunity; laws are tested against the Basic Structure and Articles 14, 19 and 21.

s: The Ninth Schedule, added in 1951 to protect agrarian reforms, has grown to about how many entries?
x: The Ninth Schedule grew to over 280 entries and is not limited to land reforms.

s: In which year was I.R. Coelho, the last word on the Ninth Schedule, decided?
x: I.R. Coelho came in 2007, after Champakam Dorairajan and the First Amendment (1951) and Minerva Mills.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: A law violating a Fundamental Right is void under Article 13
Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy
The 44th Amendment gave Directive Principles primacy over Articles 14 and 19
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights to implement Directive Principles within the basic structure
x: The attempt to give all DPSPs primacy over Articles 14 and 19 was the 42nd Amendment, struck down in Minerva Mills, not the 44th.

s: By which Amendment was Article 31C inserted into the Constitution?
x: Article 31C came with the Twenty-fifth Amendment; the Seventeenth widened 'estate' in Article 31A and dealt with land under personal cultivation.

s: What did the Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, enacted in response to Golaknath, provide?
o: The adequacy of compensation could be examined by courts.
Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
Only DPSPs could be amended by Parliament.
x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment responded to Golaknath by affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. It added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), and made presidential assent mandatory.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Twenty-fifth Amendment — inserted Article 31C and replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’
Twenty-sixth Amendment — extended Article 31C to all DPSPs
x: The Twenty-fifth Amendment replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’ and inserted Article 31C. The Twenty-fourth Amendment dealt with Parliament's amending power, the Twenty-sixth abolished privy purses, and the Forty-second extended Article 31C to all DPSPs.

s: The Twenty-fifth Amendment, 1971 was a response to which case?
x: The 25th Amendment answered R.C. Cooper (1970), replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' and inserting Article 31C.

s: Privy purses were abolished by which Amendment?
x: The 26th Amendment, 1971, responding to the Privy Purses case, abolished privy purses.

s: Which Amendment widened the meaning of 'estate' in Article 31A?
x: The 17th Amendment, 1964 widened 'estate' and allowed acquisition of land under personal cultivation only at market value.

s: Which Amendment made the adequacy of compensation non-justiciable?
x: The 4th Amendment, 1955 made adequacy of compensation non-justiciable.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Twenty-fourth Amendment, 1971:
1. It was a response to Golaknath.
2. It made the President's assent to Constitution Amendment Bills mandatory.
3. It inserted Article 31C.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 24th answered Golaknath and made the President's assent mandatory; Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment.

s: Besides Article 13(4), which clause did the 24th Amendment, 1971 add to the Constitution?
x: The 24th Amendment added Articles 13(4) and 368(3); 368(4) and (5) came with the 42nd, and 31C with the 25th.

s: Which Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all the Directive Principles?
x: The 42nd Amendment, not the 44th, attempted the extension, and it was struck down by the Supreme Court.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 31C?
o: It was introduced by the 25th Amendment in 1971
It protects laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c)
Articles 39(b) and 39(c) are the only Directive Principles that override Fundamental Rights under it
Minerva Mills upheld the 42nd Amendment's extension of it to all Directive Principles
x: Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C protection to all Directive Principles.

s: The original Article 31C protected laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under which Articles?
x: The original Article 31C shielded such laws from Articles 14, 19 and 31, and put the declaration that they implemented the policy beyond judicial question.

s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down?
o: The first part protecting laws for Articles 39(b) and 39(c)
The second part excluding judicial review
x: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second part, which excluded judicial review.

s: The continued operation of the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, was reaffirmed in which of the following decisions in 2024?
x: The Property Owners Association decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues in force.

s: Besides striking down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C, what did Minerva Mills hold about a proclamation of Emergency?
x: Minerva Mills (1980) also held that an Emergency proclamation is subject to judicial review.

s: In the Sanjeev Coke case (1983), what did the Supreme Court hold Article 39(b) to include?
o: Only resources owned by the Union
Only natural resources owned by States
x: Sanjeev Coke (1983) held that 39(b) includes privately owned resources, following Krishna Iyer's view.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the use of Directive Principles in interpretation?
o: Article 48A read with Article 21 supports the right to a healthy environment
Non-justiciability excludes Directive Principles from constitutional interpretation
Article 45 read with Article 21 has been used to enrich Fundamental Rights
Courts use Directive Principles to enrich Fundamental Rights
x: Non-justiciability does not exclude Directive Principles from interpretation; courts read them with Fundamental Rights, e.g. Article 48A with 21.

s: Reading Article 45 with Article 21 led to Article 21A through which Amendment?
x: DPSPs strengthened FRs: Article 45 read with 21 led to Article 21A by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

s: In which case was the balance between Parts III and IV held to be part of the Basic Structure?
x: Minerva Mills (1980) held the FR-DPSP balance to be part of the Basic Structure; absolute primacy to either destroys it.

s: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, on what does it depend whether a privately owned resource falls under Article 39(b)?
o: Its ownership by the Union Government alone
Nothing, since every private resource is automatically covered
Its nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being and concentration in private hands
Nothing, since no private resource can ever be covered
x: The Court held private ownership alone does not bring a resource within Article 39(b); it depends on the resource and its effects on the community.

s: Who wrote the 7:2 majority opinion in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024)?
x: CJI D.Y. Chandrachud wrote the nine-judge Bench's majority; it rejected Justice Krishna Iyer's 1977 Ranganatha Reddy minority view.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the judicial history of Article 39(b)?
o: Property Owners Association held that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b)
In Ranganatha Reddy (1977), Justice Krishna Iyer's minority view included privately owned resources in 'material resources of the community'
The broad view was followed in Sanjeev Coke (1983)
Property Owners Association was decided in 2024
x: The 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected the proposition that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b).

s: In the Ranganatha Reddy case (1977), who gave the minority view that Article 39(b) includes all privately owned resources?
x: Krishna Iyer's minority view in Ranganatha Reddy was rejected in Property Owners Association (2024), written by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud.

s: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) was decided by a Bench of how many judges?
x: A 9-judge Bench decided it by a 7:2 majority on 5 November 2024.

s: The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted which of the following?
o: Part IVB containing Article 51B and clauses (a) to (k)
Part IVA containing Article 51A and clauses (a) to (j)
x: The Forty-Second Amendment inserted Part IVA, containing the single Article 51A with clauses (a) to (j).

s: The Fundamental Duties are contained in which Part, one of the four Parts added to the Constitution after 1950?
x: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA; Parts IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA are the four Parts added after 1950.

s: Which of the following Parts was, like Part IVA, added to the Constitution after 1950?
x: The four Parts added after 1950 are IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA; Part VI deals with the States.

s: On which date did the 42nd Amendment, which inserted the Fundamental Duties, come into force?
x: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 came into force on 3 January 1977.

s: Which amendment simultaneously inserted Article 51A(g), added Article 48A and transferred forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List?
x: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted the environmental duty in Article 51A(g), added DPSP Article 48A and moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List through Entries 17A and 17B.

s: The environmental changes associated with Article 51A(g) were introduced after which international development?
x: The insertion of Article 51A(g), Article 48A and the related legislative-list changes followed the 1972 Stockholm Conference.

s: The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 is associated with which combination?
o: Insertion of Article 21A, substitution of Article 45 and addition of Article 51A(k)
Insertion of Article 32A, substitution of Article 44 and deletion of Article 51A
Insertion of Part IXA and addition of Article 51A(a)
Substitution of Article 48A and insertion of Article 51A(j)
x: The Eighty-Sixth Amendment inserted Article 21A, substituted Article 45 and added the eleventh Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k).

s: Under which Entries of the Concurrent List did the 42nd Amendment place forests and protection of wild animals and birds?
x: Along with 51A(g) and 48A, the 42nd Amendment created Entries 17A and 17B in the Concurrent List.

s: In which year was the eleventh Fundamental Duty, Article 51A(k), added to the Constitution?
x: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 51A(k), raising the number of duties from 10 to 11.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Fundamental Duties – Addressed to the State
x: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA (Article 51A) and are addressed to citizens; DPSPs are Articles 36–51.

s: How many Fundamental Duties were there immediately after the Forty-Second Amendment, and how many are there at present?
x: The Forty-Second Amendment introduced ten Fundamental Duties. The Eighty-Sixth Amendment later added clause (k), taking the total to eleven.

s: Under which Article is protection of monuments of national importance provided?
x: Protection of monuments is Article 49, a Directive Principle; 51A(h) covers scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry.

s: Under which Article is protecting the weaker sections from social injustice a directive?
x: It is not a Fundamental Duty; it is DPSP Article 46.

s: Article 48A, relating to the environment, falls under which of the following?
o: Directive Principle addressed to the State
x: Article 48A is a Directive Principle addressed to the State; the citizens' duty is in Article 51A(g), and Article 21 is read to include a clean environment.

s: Which of the following pairs is incorrectly matched?
o: Protection of public property by citizens — Article 48A
Protection of environment by the State — Article 48A
x: Protection of public property by citizens is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(i), not Article 48A. Article 48A concerns protection and improvement of the environment by the State.

s: Environmental protection appears in Directive Principle Article 48A. In which Fundamental Duty does it also appear?
x: Environment is in Article 48A and 51A(g); education links Article 45, 21A and 51A(k); heritage links Article 49 and 51A(f).

s: Which of the following appears only as a Fundamental Duty, with no look-alike in the DPSPs?
x: Scientific temper (51A(h)) is only a Fundamental Duty; environment (48A), heritage (49) and education (45) have DPSP look-alikes.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Part containing Fundamental Duties – Part IV
Committee that recommended Fundamental Duties – Swaran Singh Committee
Amendment that added Fundamental Duties – 44th Amendment, 1978
x: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the Fundamental Duties. They are in Part IV-A, Article 51-A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

s: What happened to the Swaran Singh Committee's proposal to make payment of taxes a Fundamental Duty?
x: Payment of taxes was suggested by the Committee but not accepted; 51A(i) is safeguarding public property and 51A(j) is excellence.

s: How many Fundamental Duties did the Swaran Singh Committee suggest?
x: The Committee suggested eight duties; the 42nd Amendment (1976) added ten.

s: Under the Swaran Singh Committee proposal that was not accepted, who was to prescribe penalties for non-compliance with Fundamental Duties?
x: The Committee proposed that Parliament could prescribe penalties for non-compliance; this was not accepted.

s: How many members did the Swaran Singh Committee have?
x: The Swaran Singh Committee had 12 members; it suggested 8 duties.

s: During which of the following was the need for the Swaran Singh Committee felt?
x: The Committee was set up by the Congress party in 1976 during the Internal Emergency of 1975–77, not 1962.

s: Who set up the Swaran Singh Committee of 1976, which recommended the Fundamental Duties?
x: The Congress party set up the Swaran Singh Committee in 1976, during the Internal Emergency of 1975-77.

s:
Which of the following are duties under Article 51A(i)?
1. To safeguard public property
2. To abjure violence
3. To strive towards excellence
x: Article 51A(i) asks citizens to safeguard public property and abjure violence. Striving towards excellence is clause (j).

s: Under which clause of Article 51A is renouncing practices derogatory to the dignity of women a Fundamental Duty?
x: Article 51A(e) covers harmony, common brotherhood and renouncing practices derogatory to women; 51A(d) covers defending the country.

s: Which Article contains the duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child aged six to fourteen years?
x: Article 51A(k) places this duty on a parent or guardian in respect of a child or ward aged six to fourteen years.

s: Under which clause of Article 51A is developing scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry a Fundamental Duty?
x: Clause (h) is scientific temper; (e) is harmony and dignity of women, (f) composite culture and (g) the natural environment.

s: Which clause of Article 51A asks citizens to cherish the noble ideals that inspired the freedom struggle?
x: Clause (b) covers the ideals of the freedom struggle; (a) respect for Constitution, Flag and Anthem, (c) sovereignty and integrity, (d) defence of the country.

s: Under Article 51A(g), which of the following make up the natural environment that citizens must protect?
o: Monuments and places of national importance
x: Article 51A(g) covers forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife and compassion for living creatures; it is not limited to forests and rivers.

s: Which clause of Article 51A is classified as a moral duty?
x: The moral duties are (b), (f), (h) and (j); (a), (c) and (i) are civic duties.

s: Under which Article is safeguarding public property a Fundamental Duty?
x: Article 51A(i) asks citizens to safeguard public property and abjure violence; 48A is a DPSP on the environment.

s: Under which clause of Article 51A is it a Fundamental Duty to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India?
x: Article 51A(c) asks citizens to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

s: Under which clause of Article 51A is it a Fundamental Duty to defend the country and render national service when called upon?
x: Article 51A(d) is the duty to defend the country and render national service when called upon.

s: Which clause of Article 51A asks citizens to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity?
x: Article 51A(j) is the duty to strive towards excellence so that the nation rises to higher levels of endeavour.

s: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Fundamental Duty relating to brotherhood from the Preamble?
o: Article 51A(e) refers to fraternity, while the Preamble refers to common brotherhood.
Article 51A(e) refers to harmony and common brotherhood, while the Preamble refers to fraternity.
Both provisions use only the expression 'common brotherhood'.
Neither provision contains an idea relating to brotherhood or fraternity.
x: Article 51A(e) expressly refers to harmony and common brotherhood, whereas the Preamble uses the term fraternity.

s: Critics say the Fundamental Duties are not exhaustive. Which of the following do they omit?
x: The list omits duties such as voting, paying taxes and family planning; the others are already covered.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 51A(k):
1. It was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
2. It is addressed to parents or guardians of children aged 6 to 14 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the 86th Amendment (2002) added 51A(k), the only duty addressed to parents or guardians, to give education to children aged 6-14.

s: Which of the following categories is covered by the Fundamental Duties under Article 51A?
o: Only public servants and elected representatives
Citizens and all foreign nationals residing in India
All persons, whether citizens or foreigners
x: Fundamental Duties are addressed to every citizen of India and do not extend to foreigners. This differs from certain Fundamental Rights, such as those under Articles 14, 20, 21 and 25, which are available to non-citizens as well.

s: Among the major democratic constitutions, which country is noted for having a comparable list of citizens' duties?
x: Japan's Constitution is identified as the only major democratic Constitution with a comparable list of citizens' duties. Socialist States generally give Fundamental Rights and duties relatively equal weight.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the applicability of Fundamental Duties?
o: Article 51A(k) is addressed to parents or guardians
Article 51A(i) also applies to resident foreigners
Unlike Articles 14, 20, 21 and 25, they are not open to non-citizens
x: Fundamental Duties apply only to citizens; the statement that 51A(i) binds resident foreigners is false.

s: From the Constitution of which country was the concept of Fundamental Duties taken?
x: Fundamental Duties were taken from the Constitution of the former Soviet Union (USSR). Japan only has a comparable list; Ireland is the source of DPSPs.

s: Which of the following pairs of constitutional feature and source country is correctly matched?
x: Fundamental Duties come from the former USSR, Directive Principles from Ireland and Fundamental Rights from the USA.

s: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee of 1999 was primarily concerned with which of the following?
o: Drafting a new Preamble to the Constitution
Operationalising Fundamental Duties by identifying existing legal provisions
Reviewing the federal distribution of legislative powers
Recommending the abolition of Fundamental Rights
x: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee examined ways to operationalise Fundamental Duties and identified existing laws that already gave effect to several of them.

s: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 relates to which Fundamental Duty?
o: Promote harmony and prevent caste or religious offences
Respect the National Flag and National Anthem
Protect the sovereignty and integrity of India
x: The UAPA, 1967 is linked to the duty under Article 51A(c); the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 relates to harmony.

s: Which environmental law draws on Parliament's power under Article 253 to implement international agreements?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
x: Article 253 lets Parliament legislate to implement international agreements, and it forms the constitutional basis of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

s: Through which of the following may Fundamental Duties be given legal effect?
o: Writs of constitutional courts without any law
x: Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, but legislation may enforce them and courts may refer to them in interpretation.

s: Which one of the following laws is most directly associated with giving effect to the duty to respect the National Flag, the National Anthem and the Constitution?
o: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
x: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 gives statutory effect to aspects of Article 51A(a), concerning respect for the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.

s: Courts may consider Fundamental Duties in assessing the ____ of a law restricting a Fundamental Right.
x: Courts use Fundamental Duties as an aid in judging the reasonableness of restrictions, though duties cannot override Fundamental Rights.

s: Why are the Fundamental Duties described as a 'code of moral precepts'?
o: Enforceable only during a National Emergency
Placed within Part III as enforceable rights
Non-justiciable and lacking direct constitutional sanctions
x: Because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and do not carry direct constitutional sanctions, they have been described as a code of moral precepts and, by critics, as superfluous.

s: The J.S. Verma Committee linked the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 to the duty under which Article?
x: The Protection of Civil Rights Act serves 51A(e) – harmony and no caste or religion offences.

s: In which year did the Justice J.S. Verma Committee on operationalising Fundamental Duties submit its work?
x: The J.S. Verma Committee on operationalising Fundamental Duties was in 1999; the Swaran Singh Committee was in 1976.

s: Imputations and assertions prejudicial to national integration, linked to the duty under Article 51A(c), are now an offence under which provision?
x: Such imputations are now punishable under Section 197 of the BNS, 2023 (earlier IPC Section 153B).

s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a criticism of the Fundamental Duties?
o: They are directly enforceable by courts without legislation
They are not exhaustive and omit matters such as voting and payment of taxes
Their placement as an appendage to Part IV is said to reduce their value
They are vague and ambiguous in several expressions
x: A is the odd one out: direct court enforcement without legislation is not a criticism, and it is not even true, because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable. Being not exhaustive (voting, taxes left out), placed as an appendage to Part IV, and vague are all recognised criticisms.

s: Which of the following is a recognised significance of the Fundamental Duties?
o: They provide a basis for suspending all Fundamental Rights
They can be enforced through writs
They help courts assess the reasonableness of laws
They override Fundamental Rights in a conflict
x: Fundamental Duties help courts judge the reasonableness of laws; they do not justify suspending Fundamental Rights.

s: Why do critics object to the placement of the Fundamental Duties?
o: An appendage to Part IV instead of following Part III
x: Critics say placing them as an appendage to Part IV, not after Part III, reduces their value.

s: The Supreme Court has recognised that corporations, as legal persons, may also carry which duty under Article 51A(g)?
o: To protect and improve the natural environment
To provide free and compulsory education
To preserve the composite culture of India
To promote international peace and security
x: Corporations, being legal persons, have also been held capable of carrying the duty under Article 51A(g) to protect and improve the natural environment.

s: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is presented as being correlative with which Fundamental Duty?
o: The duty to develop scientific temper
The duty to provide educational opportunities to children
The duty to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
The duty to preserve the rich heritage of composite culture
x: Rights and duties are treated as complementary. Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) is linked with the duty under Article 51A(c) to uphold and protect India's sovereignty, unity and integrity.

s: In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, to which Article was CSR including environmental protection linked?
x: The case held that CSR includes environmental protection and linked the principle to the Fundamental Duty in Article 51A(g).

s: Which case held that Fundamental Duties cannot override Fundamental Rights and that respect for national symbols needs no compelled participation?
o: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
x: In Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), the Court held Fundamental Duties cannot override Part III rights.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that rights and duties are correlative and that Fundamental Duties are as important as Fundamental Rights?
o: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India
x: In AIIMS Students' Union (2002), the Court held that rights and duties are correlative and that duties are as important as rights. Bijoe Emmanuel held that duties cannot override Fundamental Rights. Minerva Mills concerns the FR-DPSP balance. M.K. Ranjitsinh linked CSR to the environmental duty in 51A(g).

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Fundamental Duty – Automatically overrides a Fundamental Right
x: Articles 25 and 26 relate to freedom of religion, which Fundamental Duties cannot curtail; Article 48A is a Directive Principle, a duty of the State.

s: Which jurist described others holding back from interfering with a right as a duty?
x: Holland explained that others holding back from interfering is called a duty, reflecting that rights and duties are correlative.

s: Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, CSR spending must be at least what share of average net profit?
x: CSR is at least 2% of average net profit; the SC (Mar 2026) held corporations also carry the 51A(g) duty.

s: Which case recognised a clean environment as part of Article 21?
x: Subhash Kumar (1991) read a clean environment into Article 21.

s: The constitutional amendment procedure in India was borrowed from which country?
x: India borrowed the amendment procedure from South Africa. The method of electing members of the Rajya Sabha was also borrowed from South Africa.

s: Which of the following expressions is used in Article 368 to describe Parliament’s constituent power to amend the Constitution?
o: May, in exercise of its judicial power, interpret or repeal any provision
Shall, in exercise of its constituent power, amend every provision by referendum
May, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision
May, in exercise of its legislative power, repeal only those provisions approved by the States
